preschool.title: The Finance People Who Bought an Elevator Company
preschool.lesson: Sometimes people who invest in businesses end up running ordinary businesses themselves.
paragraphs: Some finance people spend their days deciding which companies should get money.
But some decide to buy one ordinary company and run it themselves — maybe even an elevator-repair company.
So after years of fancy finance, your big job might be making sure elevators get fixed. Elevators, unfortunately, do not repair themselves.

elementary.title: The Suitcase Full of Tools
elementary.lesson: Independent sponsors raise money for one deal at a time to buy and run small businesses (often $2M–$10M in adjusted earnings); Altaline Capital Management is an example, started by mid-career veterans including Rafael Telahun from TA Associates, H.I.G. Capital and KKR.
paragraphs: Once upon a campus, suits learned how to steer,
Then many of those suits went to finance—far and near.
They learned how to move money from place to place,
To pick a good company and help it win a race.
But some of those people wanted a flatter, closer view,
Not giant buyouts, but running something true.
So they packed up a briefcase, not for hedge fund flare,
But for elevators, HOAs, small businesses that need care.
Altaline was started by veterans—Rafael Telahun among them—
From TA Associates, H.I.G. Capital, and KKR, not a whim.
Bloomberg’s Allison McNeely and Preeti Singh told how it grew,
A single-deal approach, a hopeful and speedy crew.
Investors who wanted quicker paydays raised small syndicates of cash,
Giving equity and debt to buy a firm and make a plan that’s brash.
Citrin Cooperman found these deals often earn two to ten million in adjusted pay,
So buyers look for founder-run shops where old owners want to step away.
The funny, slightly odd thing—this is the market’s little trick—
Smart graduates who wanted KKR instead took over elevator-fix.
They trade Wall Street’s glitter for grease-stained keys and a van,
And use private-equity tools to help a local business stand.

What happened? Independent sponsors raise capital deal-by-deal—pulling together small equity and debt syndicates to buy founder-run businesses (often with $2 million to $10 million of adjusted earnings). Altaline Capital Management was launched by mid-career veterans from TA Associates, H.I.G. Capital and KKR to pursue deals such as elevator maintenance and homeowners’ association management, offering quicker paydays and less leverage than larger buyout funds.

middle.title: Private Equity Comes Back Down to Earth
middle.lesson: Independent sponsors combine capital raising with hands-on ownership of small businesses.
paragraphs: Private equity is finance, but its economic promise is operational: buy a company that could be run better, improve it and eventually sell it.
Independent sponsors make that model more artisanal. They find a specific business, then raise equity and debt for that deal rather than managing a permanent pool of committed capital.
A growing supply of retiring founders and investors willing to finance lower-middle-market deals has made the model attractive to experienced private-equity professionals.

Altaline Capital Management, founded by veterans of TA Associates, H.I.G. Capital and KKR, has invested in elevator maintenance and HOA management. Levine’s joke is that elite finance can ultimately turn into the extremely concrete job of making boring companies work better.

high.title: Independent Sponsors and the Return of the Operator
high.lesson: Deal-by-deal private equity shifts professionals from abstract capital allocation toward direct operational ownership.
paragraphs: Levine frames finance as a meta-business: talented people allocate capital across companies rather than operate one company directly. Private equity partially reverses that abstraction because its value proposition is to acquire businesses and improve them.

Search funds and independent sponsors push further toward operation. An independent sponsor sources a target first, then syndicates the equity and debt required for that transaction instead of drawing from a committed blind-pool fund.
The model is benefiting from slower large-cap deal activity, constrained promotion opportunities and a supply of founder-owned businesses whose baby-boomer owners want to retire.

Altaline Capital Management illustrates the punch line. Veterans of prestigious private-equity firms left high finance and invested in businesses including elevator maintenance. The allocator of capital becomes, in a meaningful sense, an elevator-company operator.

illustration.alt: Private-equity professionals in suits inspecting an elevator with a repair technician

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Independent sponsors source a business and raise equity and debt deal by deal to acquire it.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Prestigious finance careers culminate in operating mundane businesses such as elevator maintenance.

preschool.title: The Bet Where Everything Has to Go Right
preschool.lesson: A bet with lots of things that all must happen can promise a big prize but is very hard to win.
paragraphs: Imagine a bet that only wins if your team wins AND a player hits a home run AND another player does something special.
That is called a parlay. It can promise a huge prize because it is easy for one little part to go wrong.
People like exciting giant prizes. The people taking the other side of those bets often like the math even more.

elementary.title: The Bet That Is Fun Because It Is Bad
elementary.lesson: Parlays combine many bets, creating exciting payouts and unusually favorable pricing for the people making the market.
paragraphs: Sportsbooks love parlays. Instead of betting only that the Mets win, you can bet that the Mets win AND Francisco Lindor homers AND several other specific things happen. Miss one piece and the whole bet loses.

That giant possible payout is fun. It is also why sportsbooks can charge much more for parlays than for simple bets. A basic bet is easy to compare across sportsbooks; a custom ten-part parlay is harder to comparison-shop, so its price can be worse for the customer.

Kalshi is a prediction market rather than a traditional sportsbook, but its combo bets have become huge. Bloomberg reported that combos were 36% of Kalshi contracts that month and ordinary customers had lost a net $294 million on them since the start of the year, excluding fees.

Here is the interesting market-design twist: Kalshi does not have to be the house. A customer builds a combo, and market makers get about a second to bid to take the other side. Professional trading firms can do this, but so can smaller traders with good models.
One former FanDuel trader described retail customers as wanting lottery tickets. FanDuel itself has started making markets in combos too.

So prediction markets have invented a democratic innovation: instead of only the sportsbook getting to make money selling people complicated long-shot bets, independent trading nerds can compete for the privilege too.

middle.title: Who Gets the House Edge on Kalshi Parlays?
middle.lesson: Prediction-market RFQs let competing market makers capture the economics that traditional sportsbooks usually keep for themselves.
paragraphs: Parlays are profitable because every leg must hit and because bespoke combinations are difficult for bettors to comparison-shop. That lets the seller embed a larger edge than on standardized single-game bets.
Kalshi’s combo contracts reproduce that economics but change who can capture it. When a retail user requests a combo, market makers receive an RFQ and briefly compete to quote the other side.
Bloomberg found combos had reached 36% of Kalshi contracts that month while retail-like takers had lost $294 million since the start of the year, excluding fees.
The odd democratization is that sophisticated hobbyists and algorithmic firms can earn some of the edge that a conventional sportsbook would keep. FanDuel has even joined them as a market maker.

high.title: Parlays, RFQs and the Democratization of the House Edge
high.lesson: Bespoke parlay pricing creates large margins; Kalshi’s RFQ market structure transfers some of those margins from centralized sportsbooks to competing liquidity providers.
paragraphs: Single sports bets are relatively standardized and easy to comparison-shop, which constrains sportsbook margins. Multi-leg parlays are bespoke, harder to compare and highly convex, allowing much larger embedded edges.
Kalshi’s prediction-market structure separates the venue from the counterparty. For combo contracts, an RFQ is distributed to market makers, who have roughly a second to compete for the trade.

Bloomberg reported combos at 36% of Kalshi contracts that month and $294 million of net losses by retail-like takers since the start of the year, excluding fees. The economic surplus that would traditionally accrue to a sportsbook can therefore be captured by algorithmic firms or even skilled independent traders.

Levine’s recurring white whale is the logical endpoint: if retail betting biases are systematic, perhaps a transparent fund could systematically take the unpopular, positive-expected-value side. The joke is that regulated prediction markets might turn 'being the house' into an investable strategy.

illustration.alt: A long chain of sports-bet cards leading from a bettor to several competing market makers

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Parlays bundle contingent outcomes; Kalshi uses an RFQ so market makers compete to price the customer’s combo.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Prediction markets let independent traders compete with sportsbooks for the lucrative job of taking the other side of bad retail parlays.

preschool.title: The Company That Keeps Changing Costumes
preschool.lesson: Changing a company’s trendy label does not automatically make the business better.
paragraphs: Some little public companies keep changing what they do whenever a new idea gets popular.
One year the costume says CRYPTO. The next year it says AI.
A new costume can get attention, but investors eventually ask whether the company is actually good at the new job.

elementary.title: Quick, We’re an AI Company Now
elementary.lesson: Public companies can pivot toward fashionable themes to attract investors, but a new story does not guarantee a valuable business.
paragraphs: Matt Levine has a running rule of thumb: some tiny public companies seem to change businesses whenever the hottest investing buzzword changes. Gold! Cannabis! Crypto! Whatever investors want next!
Last year, digital-asset-treasury companies were the fad. A small public company could announce that it would raise money and buy crypto, and investors might suddenly care about the stock.

Now that crypto-treasury stocks have cooled, some of those companies are pivoting to artificial intelligence. K Wave Media moved from accumulating Bitcoin toward data-center development. AlphaTON Capital, which held alternative cryptocurrencies, rebranded as Alpha Compute.
There is a perfectly respectable explanation: companies change strategy when opportunities change.

There is also Levine’s funnier explanation: perhaps their most durable corporate skill is not mining gold, distributing cannabis, holding crypto or building AI infrastructure. Perhaps it is selling stock to people who are excited about whatever word is fashionable this year.
Unfortunately, Bloomberg reported that several of the AI pivots had still fallen sharply. Apparently adding AI to the costume does not force the stock price to cooperate.

middle.title: From Crypto Treasury to AI, Right on Schedule
middle.lesson: Narrative-driven pivots can help small public companies attract capital, but investor enthusiasm and operating competence are different things.
paragraphs: Small listed companies sometimes pivot repeatedly toward whatever theme currently attracts retail capital. Levine’s running sequence includes gold, cannabis, crypto mining, pandemic products, digital-asset treasuries and now AI.
The digital-asset-treasury boom created demand for otherwise underused public-company shells because their listed shares could be sold to finance crypto purchases.
As that trade cooled, some former crypto-focused firms rebranded around data centers or AI compute. Bloomberg reported weak stock performance for several such pivots.
The joke is also a capital-markets hypothesis: the stable core competency may not be any particular operating business but the ability to tell a fashionable story and issue equity into it.

high.title: The Persistent Business Model Is Selling the Next Business Model
high.lesson: For some micro-cap issuers, public-market access can be more durable than the operating theme used to attract capital at any particular moment.
paragraphs: Levine’s recurring model of promotional micro-caps is that operating themes rotate while the financing technology remains constant. A listed shell can move from gold to cannabis to crypto to digital-asset treasury strategies and then AI as investor demand migrates.

The DAT boom was unusually convenient because the public listing itself was economically useful: companies could issue equity to buy crypto, creating a reflexive relationship between market enthusiasm and asset accumulation.
With DAT valuations under pressure, Bloomberg reported pivots such as K Wave Media toward data centers and AlphaTON Capital’s rebranding as Alpha Compute, alongside substantial share-price declines.

The cynical interpretation is not that management possesses every newly fashionable operating skill. It is that access to public equity markets is the real franchise, and the business description is the periodically refreshed marketing layer.

illustration.alt: A tiny public company changing signs from crypto to AI while investors watch

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Small public companies can use fashionable strategies and equity issuance to attract capital; changing the narrative does not ensure operating success.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: The company’s enduring expertise may be selling stock, while its supposed business changes with each fad.

preschool.title: The Work Meeting Where You Should Not Tell Every Secret
preschool.lesson: Trust exercises can be awkward when personal information is later used in workplace decisions.
paragraphs: At a work retreat, people were asked to share personal things so everyone would trust each other more.
One executive shared something private about medical treatment. Later he was fired and sued the company.
The joke is that a meeting called a trust exercise can make people wonder exactly how much they should trust it.

elementary.title: Kevin's Big Sharing Circle
elementary.lesson: Adults sometimes say things at work that get them into trouble, even when they think they are building trust.
paragraphs: In a quiet California valley, Netflix owned a ranch so grand,
Sendero Ranch held chairs in a circle on warm January land.
Executives from Eyeline Studios sat with badges and coffee in hand,
They were asked to be honest, to try something trusting and planned.
Kevin Baillie sighed, looked up, and let a small secret fall,
He told them he’d taken ketamine the doctor had given to him after all.
The circle was soft as a pillow, and everyone listened close,
But whispered things travel oddly, like petals that the wind chose.
Soon a note crossed a desk, and a question came: What did he mean?
An investigation opened, and the next scene was less serene.
Kevin had been vice president, head of creative at Eyeline’s place,
He was paid $1.1 million a year, a sum many would chase.
Because he’d spoken in that circle, Netflix looked into his claim,
They then let him go from the job, and Kevin answered back with a legal name.
It’s strange and it’s funny, the way trust exercises can twist —
You think you’re building a bridge, but sometimes bridges can’t resist
Turning private things into paper and questions that won't sleep,
And a hug in a meadow can lead to headlines that run deep.

What happened? Kevin Baillie, vice president and head of creative at Eyeline Studios, told colleagues at a January 2026 “Vulnerability-Trust” exercise at Netflix’s Sendero Ranch that he had taken medically prescribed ketamine. Netflix investigated and fired him from a $1.1 million-a-year job; Baillie has filed a lawsuit.

middle.title: Vulnerability, Trust and the Corporate Record
middle.lesson: Workplace trust exercises create tension between candid disclosure and the employer’s ability to act on information employees reveal.
paragraphs: Kevin Baillie, formerly a Netflix executive and head of creative at Eyeline Studios, sued after he said a disclosure during a 'Vulnerability-Trust exercise' contributed to an investigation and his firing.
Baillie said he disclosed medically prescribed ketamine treatment during a January 2026 retreat at Netflix-owned Sendero Ranch. The lawsuit concerns what followed and whether Netflix acted properly.

Levine turns the episode into a corporate-governance joke: an institution can encourage radical candor while employees rationally worry that candid information will affect future employment decisions.
His mock advice is to confess only to being 'too much of a perfectionist' — vulnerability engineered to contain no actual vulnerability.

high.title: The Incentive Problem in Corporate Vulnerability
high.lesson: An employer’s request for candor can conflict with employees’ rational incentives when disclosed information may affect employment decisions.
paragraphs: The Baillie lawsuit presents a classic incentive mismatch inside a modern corporate ritual. A 'Vulnerability-Trust exercise' asks employees to disclose information precisely because it is personal and consequential; the employer simultaneously remains an institution capable of investigating and terminating them.

Kevin Baillie, formerly vice president and head of creative at Netflix’s Eyeline Studios, says he disclosed medically prescribed ketamine treatment at a January 2026 retreat at Netflix-owned Sendero Ranch and was later investigated and fired. He sued Netflix.

Whatever the legal merits, Levine focuses on mechanism design: asking for authentic vulnerability without credible limits on how disclosures will be used may produce performative vulnerability instead.
Hence his joke confession — 'Sometimes I’m too much of a perfectionist' — which perfectly satisfies the ritual while revealing nothing useful at all.

illustration.alt: Executives in a retreat circle beneath a Trust Exercise sign while one person cautiously raises a hand

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: This section is primarily about workplace incentives rather than a financial instrument.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: A corporate exercise asking employees to trust the company becomes evidence for why they might not want to trust the company.
